extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotle; readers studying moral and political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and interpretation of Aristotle's account of the Chief Good (Happiness), the role of Pleasure, the highest form of life, and related political/moral theory in the Nicomachean Ethics. Targets students and general readers of classical ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as concomitant and index of activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is the natural concomitant and index of perfect activity, distinguishable but inseparable from it—'the activity of a subject at its best acting upon an object at its best.' It is therefore always and in itself a good, though its value rises and falls with that of the activity with which it is conjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure should be evaluated in relation to the activity it accompanies: pleasures tied to higher activities are more valuable. Do not treat pleasure in isolation; assess the worth of the corresponding activity to judge the pleasure's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest pleasures accompany highest activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest and best pleasures are those which accompany the highest and best activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ranking pleasures, prioritize those that are inseparable from superior intellectual or virtuous activities. This rules out equating mere sensual enjoyment with the highest human goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is necessary but not the whole of the best life
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is a necessary element in the best life but it is not the whole of it nor the principal ingredient. The value of a life depends upon the nature and worth of the activity which it involves; given the maximum of full free action, the maximum of pleasure necessary follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the presence of pleasure with a life being the best possible; evaluate the constitutive activities first.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Happiness is contemplative life
rubrics_metrics.description: True Happiness (great satisfaction) is to be found in the life of the onlooker, the disinterested spectator — 'in the life of the philosopher, the life of scientific and philosophic contemplation.' The highest and most satisfying form of life possible to man is the contemplative life, conceived as intense, ceaseless intellectual activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lives by their capacity for contemplative intellectual activity. Practical or political excellence may be valuable but is secondary to the contemplative ideal in Aristotle's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/moral life is secondary for highest Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical or moral life (the life of the citizen, soldier, or statesman) is not the locus of True Happiness in the highest sense; it is only in a secondary sense, and for those incapable of contemplation, that the practical or moral ideal is the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When contrasting life-forms, treat political/moral excellence as important but subordinate when judging the absolute highest human good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical caveats about the contemplative ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's account of the contemplative life has shortcomings: (1) its relation to the lower practical ideal is left somewhat obscure; (2) its realisation seems possible only to a gifted few under exceptional circumstances; (3) its content appears unnecessarily and unjustifiably limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the contemplative ideal, be mindful of practical limits, inclusivity concerns, and the need to clarify its connection to ordinary moral life.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and law should embody best reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The State, operating through Law (Reason backed by Force), is the great agency in producing the best life. Ideally the best reason of the community should be embodied in its laws; where that is not possible, anyone who would make himself and others better must become a 'miniature legislator' and study principles of law, morality, and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political arrangements and legislation by how well they incorporate and promote the community's best reason and the conditions for good lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral philosophy is teleological (eudaimonistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's Moral Philosophy is essentially teleological: every human practical activity is directed towards a simple End discoverable by reflection, and this End is conceived as the object of universal human desire — enjoyment or Happiness — not the fulfilment of Duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess actions and institutions by their conduciveness to the final end (Happiness) rather than by mere formal duties; measure value by contribution to flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right action presupposes thinking that reveals the situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Right action presupposes thought or thinking: not merely imaginative forecasting or calculation of means to ends, but thinking which reveals to the agent both the universal situation and the ever-varying particular situation in which he acts. In such knowledge of given or historic fact lie the natural determinants of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practical reasoning by its sensitivity to both general principles and concrete, particular circumstances; avoid reducing moral thought to mere instrumental calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on means-end distinction in morality
rubrics_metrics.description: The application to morality of the distinction of means and end can mislead: in morality everything is both means and end, so thinking that presupposes a rigid separation tends to error. Moral thinking that matters is not merely calculation but discernment of the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging actions, recognize the interdependence of ends and means; be cautious of approaches that treat moral ends as wholly separable from means.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Chief Good (Happiness) must be final and self-sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Good is something final (an object of choice always in itself and never as a means) and self-sufficient (taken alone it makes life choice-worthy and to be in want of nothing). Happiness is manifestly something final and self-sufficient, the end of all things which are and may be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'finality' and 'self-sufficiency' as tests when proposing candidates for the highest human good: does the candidate satisfy both criteria and make life choice-worthy on its own?

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy and characterization of ends (final vs instrumental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ends are many and some are chosen with a view to others (instrumental). The absolutely final is that which is chosen always for itself and never as a means. The Chief Good, if unique, must be the most final among ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating aims of arts, sciences, or life-practices, classify ends as final or instrumental and identify which is most 'absolutely final' for human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: The work of man is rational activity
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the Chief Good we must discover the work of man. It is not mere life (shared with plants) nor mere sensation (shared with animals) but a life of the Rational Nature; specifically, the activity of the rational part of the soul — 'a kind of life of the Rational Nature apt to act.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge human excellence and happiness by whether a life realizes the distinctive human function: rational activity in accordance with virtue or excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of students for Moral Philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The young man is not a fit student of Moral Philosophy, for he has no experience in the actions of life, and, being apt to follow passions, will often hear as though he heard not. Those formed in habits and self-control will profit most from moral instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider maturity and experience when teaching or assessing understanding of practical ethics; emphasize formation of habits and self-control prior to abstract moral theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical attainability of the Good
rubrics_metrics.description: The Good we seek must be something attainable and practical for human life; knowledge of an abstract 'very-good' that is not concrete or attainable would be of little practical use to artisans or agents who need to heal individuals or command armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When positing ultimate goods or ideals, require that they be concretely relevant and attainable in ordinary human practice, not merely abstract metaphysical entities.
